subsubtopic: CRASH OF PWA AIRCRAFT AT CRANBROOK, B.C.-LIABILITY FOR CLAIMS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgency and concern to a number of Canadians. It has now been some 14 weeks without settlement of claims of the surviving families of those killed in the crash of the PWA Boeing jet at Cranbrook on February 11.
In light of the agreement that came out during the coroner's inquiry among counsel for Pacific Western Airlines, the Boeing Aircraft Company, the manufacturer of the reverse thrusters, the town of Cranbrook and others to pool the liability so that claims might be at least partially settled, thereby relieving the undue financial distress caused by this accident, and in light of the failure of this proposal being implemented because of refusal by counsel for the Ministry of Transport, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco):
That this House direct counsel for the Ministry of Transport to immediately review its position with respect to the pooling of liability so that some measure of relief from the Financial burden imposed on these families may be realized.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, that being the mounting crisis in Canada's grain industry reflected in what as of this week amounts to a one million ton backlog in shipping. Ships are now waiting to load grain in all Canadian ports-Vancouver,
Thunder Bay and on the St. Lawrence. Because of the seriousness of this matter, which will reflect itself in lower quota levels, a larger than expected carry-over of western Canadian grain, and demurrage charges that will be the highest on record, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton):
That the government immediately pass an order in council freeing money for the 4,000 grain hopper cars the Canadian Wheat Board has requested and launch immediately into a boxcar rehabilitation program.

We have the capacity to move a lot of grain, but we are not satisfied with that because we believe there will be more grain, and a need for more, and we will continue to move it.
I find it odd that the hon. member now comes down against his colleague in criticizing financial support for the rebuilding of the rail lines. This is not a gift to the railways; it is a transfer of funds to obtain a very specific upgrading of branch lines like the Conquest line which was completed during the course of last summer, and hundreds of thousands of miles of line which will be completed during the course of this summer. It is far less than the transfer we would make to the railways if we had carried out literally the recommendation of the Hall commission report which has just been urged upon me by a variety of colleagues. That would have seen twice as much money per year go to the railways, without the commitment in relation to upgrading unless we had actually put in more money. We are getting exact results for our dollars, whether in hopper cars or rebuilt lines, when we spend the dollars to get the results.

Mr. Speaker, to put the matter in perspective, I am quoting figures from the minister's own publication put out by the Canadian Wheat Board entitled "Grain Matters". [Mr. Lang.)
only maintain an adequate fleet but will ensure that that fleet is operative at all times?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very gist of the recommendations of Hall and Snavely in this regard were that the government should pay the railways enough money so that they would in fact be able to operate at a profit in this area. They would have had us transfer the money without strings attached. The railways, of course, have been letting their systems deteriorate. Without the cash which the Snavely and Hall commissions found them to be short of, they have not been rebuilding cars. Thus, in 1972 and at intervals since that time this government has been taking action by buying hopper cars and putting them in place.

speechtext: MR. BASFORD-FINANCE-ALLEGATIONS MADE BY HON. MEMBER FOR YORK-SIMCOE REGARDING SPECULATION ON DOLLAR BY MPs

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yesterday, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) raised by way of a question of privilege certain remarks which were attributed to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), who indicated that he would be here today. I understand he now wishes to contribute to that subject.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege relating to the matter raised yesterday in this House by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I regret I was not in the House yesterday to deal with the subject when it was first raised, but I had made three commitments in my home area which I simply could not cancel at the last minute. In fact I did not know there would be a question of privilege raised until noon yesterday at which time I had left my first meeting and was heading for my second meeting of the day.
The proposed questions of privilege raised by the two members concern a report carried by the Canadian Press news agency last Friday night in which I was quoted as saying:
We've learned through the banks that nine Liberal MPs played the Canadian dollar as it was going down.
That report originated from a lengthy 90 minute interview I had Thursday last with a Canadian Press reporter. During the course of our discussion reference was made to the circumstances in which charges are or are not made in this House. I gave two examples of charges that we had made only after we were satisfied we had concrete evidence to make our point. On the other hand, as an example of a situation which I had not raised here, I mentioned that we had received the above reports to the effect that as many as nine Liberal MPs, and there were supposed to be two or three cabinet ministers in the nine, had speculated against the Canadian dollar, but that I had not pursued the question in the House. I said that because as yet I had not been able to obtain concrete evidence to substantiate those reports.
Mr. Speaker, that was a true and honest statement. I had received such information from what I considered to be credible sources. And I had decided not to raise the matter in the House unless and until I had concrete evidence.
It may be helpful if I read into the record a partial transcript of what the Canadian Press reported me to have said. In their report they quote me as stating:
There are things we could be mentioning, that we have not mentioned. I'm very curious about some of these things. Like I noticed Trudeau twice has said 
about opposition members trading on the Canadian dollar. I don't know whether you've noticed that.
Who was the member that shouted out to me yesterday, "Are you buying Canadian dollars?"
I don't know why they say that. Because we've learned through the banks that nine Liberal MPs played the Canadian market as it was going down.
Q: Were they named?
Stevens: Not to me. But apparently the names are available. But we've been in a real dilemma as to whether we should press it or whether we should just let it lie. I don't know.
I cannot understand why Trudeau would be inferring that we were doing it, other than whatever guilty conscience he's got, eh?
The two references I was referring to in connection with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appear in Hansard, one on February 16, page 2914. The statement I would like to read into the record was in answer to a question put by myself with respect to the desirability of an 80-cent dollar. The Prime Minister stated, and I quote:
The hon. member knows that if I were to give an answer, it would set up a wave of speculation which he and his friends might perhaps make money out of, but that is not our intention.
In response to a question put to the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), again dealing with the 80-cent dollar, asking whether there was some policy to hold it at that level, the Prime Minister stated, as recorded at page 4192 of Hansard for April 6, and I quote:
It is a floating dollar. I understand hon. members opposite would like to engage in a bit of speculation; they would like us to tell them the way it will float. If they want to risk some money, they can do it on their own.
Those are the two references I referred to in the Canadian Press interview. I could have also mentioned an exchange that took place on November 9, mainly involving the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). This exchange appears at pages 758 and 759 of Hansard, and I quote:
Tell us about the dollar.

Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, on reflection I was wrong even to raise the matter of dollar speculation with the CP reporter, even in the context of explaining why I had not pursued it in the House. I made statements which I now realize constituted an allegation or are perceived as an allegation which I cannot substantiate at this time.
That being the case, Mr. Speaker, and in keeping with the established practice, I wish to withdraw any such allegation against any member of this House. While I made no reference to any individual member, I regret any embarrassment which I have caused to any hon. member of this chamber.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to listen to what the hon. member for Simcoe North had to say. He has, I take it, given you, Mr. Speaker, and the House an unqualified and unconditional withdrawal and retraction of any remarks made by him with regard to speculating on the dollar. I am pleased that we on this side raised the question of privilege and that this matter is now cleared up. I would, however, observe that we have seen a somewhat slick performance this afternoon.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I have before me a procedural matter to decide. The question was raised by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) yesterday as a matter of privilege and, as I have said many times in the past, there is no machinery available whereby I can call upon the same member to contribute twice to the same question. In some circumstances I extend that opportunity, at least in a nominal way; there are occasions, such as today, when the House has given an hon. member the option to withdraw a remark or make an apology. In such cases it is not at all extraordinary, I think, to allow some indication from the original mover of the motion that the apology has been accepted as put forward. In that sense I thought it appropriate on this occasion to recognize the original mover of the motion. However, on strict procedural grounds I ought not to accept a second contribution on the same question of privilege by any member, and that is a rather safe course to follow.
The second point I wish to make is that during the course of the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) I was weighing the information he was presenting to the House, and I must say I came to precisely the same conclusion as he did. He had an explanation for his remarks; that he had put them forward in a somewhat strict context. His explanation was this was an example of a case which he would not pursue in the House because he lacked evidence, and in doing so-as he realized on reflection-that in itself was an indiscretion which had rather heavy consequences for the reputation of the House in general. I was, of course, very pleased that he had come to the same conclusion as I had, and I felt he had done entirely the honourable thing in reaching that conclusion and extending his apologies.
Privilege-Mr. F. Hamilton
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In any case, my opinion of the course he followed is not important, except in a procedural sense. The hon. member made these allegations outside the House. He was the subject, as a result, of two motions, one put forward by the Minister of Justice and the other by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). With respect to those motions the hon. member came in to make his contribution today and, again in a procedural sense, having made his apology for the action he took in making those allegations, and having withdrawn those allegations, the matter is now totally closed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is raised at this time because the evidence upon which it is based was only available to me minutes before one o'clock today. Otherwise I would have given Your Honour the usual notice. I would like to report that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) has given answers in this House which appear to have been misleading. I am not quite certain of the appropriate parliamentary language, but I can say that the answers he has given are not the truth. I brought this matter up a week ago on a point of order. It has become more explicit with the passage of time, and I believe it now qualifies as a question of privilege.
Your Honour will recall that on May 8 the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) asked a question about the neutron bomb. The minister answered with respect to another subject, nuclear missiles. He said, "We do not have any nuclear weapons, nor would they be deployed on our soil." I asked the minister about this a week later and strangely enough he said to me, "I believe the hon. member knows I do not answer questions on that subject." That was after I had asked him about the previous question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood. This served only to confuse himself and perhaps the House. It certainly did not mislead me, but it seemed to be an attempt to mislead the House.
He at the same time tried to cast a certain aspersion on a previous minister of national defence by saying that the previ-

ous minister had not answered questions on that subject. He said, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I believe my predecessor neither confirmed nor denied such allegations.
A few minutes later, as Your Honour will recall, I brought the record into the House and showed where the previous minister had stated that, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, none of our aircraft are equipped with nuclear missiles, but we do have in storage, and this has been public knowledge for several years- nuclear missiles at Comox and at the other bases from which our interceptor squadrons take off.
I would like to read a news report put out by Broadcast News. It starts off as follows:
Danson-Nuclear
Ottawa-Defence Minister Barney Danson has confirmed reports there are nuclear weapons in Canada.
The minister has refused on several occasions in the past to comment. However, he told Broadcast News in Ottawa today that Canadian planes attached to the North American Air Defence Command have nuclear capabilities. Danson said the aircraft are stationed at Comox, British Columbia. However, he would not say how many nuclear weapons are on Canadian soil, their size, or their capabilities.
But the minister says the weapons will be returned to the United States when Canada gets its new fighter aircraft. Danson said the nuclear weapons were needed because Canada's aging fighters weren't a credible deterrent with conventional weapons.
However, Danson said the new planes will be so sophisticated they won't need nuclear capabilities.
A large part of the release is true, although it did miss the point in a parliamentary sense. The point here is that on May 8 the minister said that we do not have any nuclear weapons, nor would they be deployed on our soil, and in this Broadcast News release he confirmed reports that there are nuclear weapons in Canada. The minister may have thought he was doing what he did for security reasons, or perhaps because of ignorance of the facts.
I do not know how many people, if any, were misled. It depends upon how many people believe the minister when he speaks about defence matters. However, it is a clear case of misleading the House, and I believe the minister should apologize to the House. If he does not, I am prepared to move a motion that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speechtext: The House resumed, from May 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-56, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole, and of the amendment (Mr. Broadbent) (p. 5548).

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was just over a month ago that I expressed my concern in this House during the budget debate about the potential for damage to our federal system when one level of government fails to consult and reach accord with the other, and the past few weeks have indeed shown that my fears were justified.
- The process of consultation between levels of government is vital to any federal state, but it is an absolute imperative in matters relating to fiscal measures, especially when federal initiatives affect the fiscal planning of the provincial governments. I say that, sir, because the provinces are responsible for the collection of something like 60 per cent of the public revenues in Canada, and for about 60 per cent of total public expenditures. That being the case, they have a heavy responsibility to plan their financial affairs carefully. Their budgets are not something that can be thrown together at the last moment, and yet in the instance that we have before us in consideration of this bill we have the federal government intervening in the financial planning of the provinces in a capricious and arbitrary way. Capricious and arbitrary intervention is what we have witnessed throughout this entire sales tax fiasco, a fiasco that has gone from bad to worse over the past month.
Let us take a look at how the government has managed, in the few weeks since it introduced its budget, to turn bungling into disaster, incompetence into disunity. The original proposal put forward on budget night was for the provinces to agree to reduce their sales tax and, in return, to be compensated by a
Income Tax Act
transfer of federal income tax into their treasuries. This proposal required consultation and negotiation with the provincial governments affected. Consultation to some degree there may have been; negotiation there was not, even though it was in a field of provincial jurisdiction.
The federal government apparently decided in advance that the only acceptable variation to its proposal would be a minor one, that is, it would agree to lengthen the time to three months and reduce the amount of the sales tax cut. The more affluent provinces were required to pick up one third of the cost of the reduction. That proposal, as the Minister of Finance (Mr.Chretien) stressed in his press conference on the night of the budget speech, was not disclosed in full, as a matter of policy, to any province until two or three hours before the minister spoke in the House of Commons that night.
The other provinces which were bringing down their budgets that night, namely, British Columbia and Manitoba, had to wait until the Minister of Finance confirmed his proposals in the budget speech itself before they could vary their own budgets to take that initiative into account. Indeed the Minister of Finance pointed out in a television broadcast last Sunday that, as of budget day, all he had discussed with the provinces was, as he put it, a hypothetical situation. "If I were to do such and such", he said to the provinces, "what would you think?" That was what the minister stated at the press conference last Sunday.
Those provinces which were in the process of drawing up their own budgets for presentation the same night had to plan for two possibilities: one, if the Minister of Finance proceeded with his proposal, and another, if he did not. Manitoba is a case in point. Being just one hour behind Ottawa's time, Manitoba's minister of finance was getting ready to present his budget as the federal minister's budget speech was being made in the House of Commons. The Manitoba minister of finance, Mr. Craik, had his two possibilities ready: one, if Ottawa proceeded, and the other, if it did not. So as he began the presentation of his own budget his aides were required to monitor the budget proposals of the Minister of Finance in Ottawa to ensure that the sales tax proposals had indeed been included in the budget presentation. Only then, by monitoring what the Minister of Finance in Ottawa had said, could Manitoba's minister of finance include in his presentation a special section that would ensure that the two budgets dealt simultaneously with the sales tax proposal. That is what consultation really amounted to.
In these circumstances there was precious little time for manoeuvrability or even for consideration on the part of that particular province, and certainly none for meaningful consultation about a proposal that was finally made firm, but made firm only on the night that the Minister of Finance presented his budget.
The consultation of which the Minister of Finance has boasted in the House must have been casual, informal, and indefinite in the extreme for such a situation, such a scenario as the one that I have described, to have been allowed to develop.

The provincial ministers of finance throughout the country thought something was coming. It had been indicated to them that something was coming, but they had no assurance that in fact anything would be coming until the Minister of Finance made the announcement in his budget speech. The consultation of which he boasted amounted to this. A proposal was made; the provinces were told that one variation to it would be acceptable, all other variations would be rejected out of hand. That is indeed what happened. It was: take it with or without this slight modification, or leave it. As I have already pointed out, according to the minister's own statement the discussions ' until then had been about a purely hypothetical situation.
The minister of finance in the province of Quebec was in a different position from his colleagues in the other provinces because he had a manoeuvrability that they lacked. Since he was the only minister of finance whose budget had not been brought down by April 10, he was able to consider a concrete proposal rather than a hypothetical one, and he had time to advance a counter-proposal.
Would anyone in this House, with the possible exception of the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), believe that Mr. Parizeau would fail to take advantage of that opportunity? Why did the Minister of Finance proceed without the agreement of the Quebec minister of finance? Since the date of the Quebec budget had been announced well in advance, why did this government not wait for the Quebec minister of finance to show his hand before they showed theirs? One can only surmise that the reason they did not wait was a political one. They were attempting to provoke a confrontation with the government of Quebec to shore up their position for the election campaign that they have been orchestrating throughout the winter and early spring. The reason a budget was brought down in this House on April 10 was to provide a platform for the Liberal party in that election, an election that they never did get around to calling.
Hear, hear!

That platform would have been one which could be presented as an attempt to co-ordinate federal-provincial fiscal policies and to stimulate the economy. Also they could claim the attempt was being resisted by the separatist provincial government in Quebec. That was their game, and that is what they set out to try to achieve. Obviously hon. members opposite knew the advantage and value of having a convenient enemy.
In its calculation of this Machiavellian strategy, the government ignored the fact that the province of Quebec, like every other province, had a legitimate right to resist this proposal or to modify it, since it dealt with an area of unquestioned provincial jurisdiction. As has been said on many occasions throughout the history of parliamentary democracy-this edict has been said over and over again-"the right to tax is the right to govern." For the federal government to attempt to dictate the manner in which a province raises, lowers or

abolishes its sales taxes, is to violate that basic democratic principle.
Hear, hear!

As for the other provinces, for reasons having to do with their desire to co-ordinate fiscal policy, or because the proposal promised benefits to their people, they, with greater or less degrees of reluctance, chose to co-operate with the federal government's initiative. This was not an easy decision for them to make. Whereas an across the board sales tax reduction throughout Canada would benefit consumers in all provinces with such taxes, it would disproportionately benefit those provinces with disproportionate shares of Canada's manufacturing capacity. Moreover, each province, except the Atlantic provinces, was being asked to re-order its priorities to pay one third of the cost of this reduction. In other words, the province of Saskatchewan, for example, was paying out money to subsidize not only its own consumers, but also the manufacturing sector in British Columbia or in Ontario. There is no question that this proposal would provide-and indeed it may have been designed to provide-more benefits to some provinces than to others.
Mr. Parizeau's decision was an attempt to ensure that the people of Quebec obtained full benefit for whatever sales tax reductions were made as part of this package. While his motives in doing so may have been questionable, his proposals are based on an undoubted and important provincial right. That is why his proposals have been supported by all the parties in the Quebec national assembly and by almost all shades of public opinion in the province of Quebec, ranging from separatist to staunchly federalist. His proposals undoubtedly were designed also to place the federal government in a most embarrassing position. They have succeeded in doing so.
The federal government obtained the consent of the other provinces to this scheme on the understanding that the sales tax cuts would be across the board in all the provinces, but the Quebec government legitimately challenged whether that uniformity should be forced on them. Then the federal government had to decide whether to accept the modifications proposed by Mr. Parizeau, or to exclude the province of Quebec from its initiative. Instead of confronting this dilemma, the Minister of Finance has attempted to make an end run around it. This attempt was made by using the federal taxing power to rebate directly to the taxpayers of Quebec a sum of money equivalent to the value of the sales tax cuts which the minister refuses to negotiate with the government of Quebec, the sum of $186 million. Now we are faced with a situation which almost perfectly illustrates a concern raised in the abstract some nine years ago during the discussions on constitutional review.
I should like to refer to some of the arguments raised during the period of the constitutional review between 1966 and 1971. For a long time there had been a consensus among the provinces on the need to manage their own fiscal affairs, to do so without the intervention of the federal government. Also there was a consensus that they should have the right to obtain
May 24, 1978

their revenues in the way they judge consistent with their fiscal needs, and to spend those moneys on projects of high priority to them.
In 1969 when the federal government began to recognize the force of some of these arguments during that constitutional review, the question of using federal fiscal muscle to regiment the provinces into line came up for broad discussion. In those discussions, the Trudeau government acknowledged the desirability of limitations on its spending power. Simultaneously it made proposals about what to do when a province did not want to join a scheme to which most of the other provinces had formally and officially agreed. At that time the Trudeau government proposed making payments directly to individuals, a proposal which was attacked by the provinces, including those which are strong supporters of a vigorous central government.
I should like to refer to a few of the arguments made by the premiers against that federal proposal to make payments direct to individuals. Mr. Smallwood, the then premier of Newfoundland, said the following:
Has it ever been done and ought it to be done? If there is to be a federal redistribution of income surely it ought to be on a national basis and not provincial.
He went on to say that, if it is to be provincial, it must be done by the legislature of the province.
Mr. Robarts, the then premier of Ontario, said the following:
If you do attempt to return the money to the individuals in the province, we must realize, of course, that you are not going to return it to the people who paid the tax.
He continued by indicating that it simply would not be exact, and asked the following:
Are you going to return it just to taxpayers or to every single individual?
That was his question. It is very relevant today.
Mr. Bennett, the then premier of British Columbia, perhaps signified the danger of the federal proposal most clearly back in 1969 when he made the following statement:
You are going to play provincial governments against the federal government and you are going to break up this country and not build up Canadian unity. You are going to make for disunity.
Therefore the proposal of the federal government to proceed by direct payments to individuals, in the way it is proceeding now, was tabled by the Prime Minister, who said the following:
I think the views have been fully aired all around and the most we can do at this time is to let them lie there until further meetings. There is nothing to add to that.
Indeed, he did not add anything either at the Victoria constitutional conference or subsequently. The federal government's method of dealing with this kind of impasse was discussed back in 1969 and was rejected by the provinces at that time. Also it was rejected by the joint parliamentary committee on the constitution in 1972. That proposal has now been resurrected unilaterally by the Minister of Finance.

Why has that been done, Mr. Speaker? I suggest it is for two reasons. The first is, it is his attempt to regain the initiative in the bungled confrontation he deliberately staged with the province of Quebec. That motivation is understandable, if contemptible. But the second motive of the Minister of Finance in putting forward this proposal is to extend the use of the federal spending power by deliberate invasion of provincial control of the sales tax field. That motive would be understandable only if we were to assume that the government is an agent provocateur working on behalf of the cause of separatism. What better strategy could the proponents of separatism conceive than to have the federal government boldly stake out a claim to use the federal spending power to bludgeon provincial governments whenever an impasse was reached between them and Ottawa?
The minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are acting in such a way as to give an aura of credibility to the image of confederation which the Parti Qu6becois has desperately, and to this point with diminishing success, tried to portray as reality to the people of Quebec; an image of an aggressive, centralizing, power hungry government at Ottawa, eager to grasp every opportunity to destroy the exising balance of federalism and to move Canada toward a unitary state.
Someone, somehow, must get it through the heads of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that Canadian nationalism and the cause of federalism in the province of Quebec will best be promoted by wise and effective use of the powers now enjoyed by the federal government, not by a backstairs usurpation of the powers assigned by the constitution to the provinces.
Claude Ryan, the Leader of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, put that case so succinctly when he said in an interview last Sunday that the strength of the Parti Quebecois "has definitely been helped by the federal government's stubborn position".
This view is reinforced by a Quebec journalist, Don McGill-vary, writing in the Montreal Gazette on May 23 in these words:
And Chritien and Prime Minister Trudeau seem to be unaware still that they are giving federalism a bad name. Quebeckers may well be persuaded to stay in confederation if they feel that the rights of their province will be guaranteed and respected.
But if the future that Ottawa holds out to them is a succession of episodes of federal meddling, like that of the past few weeks, the case for independence is bound to seem more persuasive.
That is the kind of result this federal government may well promote.
The direct tax rebate is not only a dangerous innovation, but one unprecedented in our history and which strikes at the very balance of confederation. Not only is it dangerous, and not only does it strike at the balance of confederation, it is also very meanly conceived. It calculates that for an S85 cheque the taxpayers of Quebec will abandon the option of looking to their provincial government, whatever political stripe that government might be, to defend the existing distribution of

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
powers under the constitution. It presupposes that $85 is the asking price for the loyalty of Quebeckers.
It is no longer good enough, according to those opposite, to be a federalist in the province of Quebec unless one's definiton of federalism precisely and on every point coincides exactly with their own. That kind of rigid "them and us" approach calls into question the very basis of federal-provincial relations. It is one of the key reasons why it is becoming more and more clear that this government is part of the problem and not part of the solution to the problem of national unity.
And what has this face-saving proposal in the bill done to the economic initiative which was supposed to have been the point of this whole exercise? What has it done to the original budget proposal? It has, literally speaking, turned that proposal on its head. Instead of a sales tax cut which benefits all consumers, what the Minister of Finance proposes is a direct income tax rebate in one province; a rebate which discriminates against those too poor to pay income taxes, and which favours those most likely to save rather than spend the rebate they would receive. That tendency to save is exactly what the minister wanted to avoid in the first place.
Here is what the minister had to say in this regard at his press conference on the night he presented his budget:
It is an economic package to restore confidence, to stimulate demand very quickly. That was the aim ... to increase demand in the Canadian economy. The other tax cuts available to me were of a different nature and we were not sure that they would go to the people who spend their money. Income tax? Perhaps the people would have put that money in savings.
This, suggests the minister, is what went wrong with his earlier income tax cut. The people saved it and did not spend it, but the sales tax cut, he promised, would be different. Again I quote from the press conference on the night the minister presented his budget:
This retail sales tax is going to everyone who spends his money. Even those who don't pay any income tax, the poor in the society, will get a benefit in spending their money.
In the context of the minister's statement that night about his budget, Mr. Parizeau's proposal bears a closer resemblance to the avowed purpose of the budget initiative than the provisions of the bill we are debating here today. Mr. Parizeau's proposal benefits all the consumers in the province of Quebec, rich and poor, and it directly stimulates purchasing in that province, and that was what the Minister of Finance said on budget night he wanted to do. How he has turned that proposal around! Since no province has a complete monopoly on any industry, the proposal which is put forward in the province of Quebec at this time benefits manufacturers in many other provinces of Canada. The effect is disproportionately beneficial to Quebec, to be sure, but the effect of the original budget proposal, as I have already noted, is in itself disproportionately beneficial to those provinces in which manufacturing is concentrated.
However ingenious may be the rationalizations of those opposite for their course of action, however many red herrings they may wish to lay across their trail of blundering, arrogance, stupidity, and cynical political manipulation, they will

never convince anyone that they are the victims rather than the authors of their own misfortune. That fact would ordinarily be of concern only to those interested in an attractive image for the Liberal party. But in this case the stakes are far more serious. By their approach to all provinces in formulating their original proposal, by the action they have taken to punish the one province which chose not to go along, and by their arrogant assumption of the right to use the federal spending power to expand clandestinely the area of federal authority, they have put the Government of Canada in a position of saying to every province implicitly, "That we will do what we like regardless of the constitution, with your consent if possible, without it if necessary".
That position is objectionable not just to the Parti Quebe-cois, not just to the province of Quebec, not just to provincial governments everywhere, but to every Canadian who believes in a federal system of government. Their position does not even have the merit of candour. The federal government is saying in effect, "We believe in a unitary state, we know that is unacceptable, but we are going to move toward that goal at every opportunity."
I could respect a government that wanted to change the federal system radically to centralize power and jurisdictions at Ottawa, much as I would disagree with that position. But what I cannot respect, and what I protest against with real anger, is a government that professes to defend federalism while undermining it at every opportunity, whenever it believes it can confuse or frighten the people of Canada into going along with it.
Canadians need a government at the federal level that is strong, dynamic, and effective. Those qualities flow from imagination, vigour, and ability. They do not come from attempts to weaken the other partners in the federal system, but from making good and efficient use of the powers and the opportunities which the federal government itself holds. The federal government will be respected in Canada when it respects the rights of the provinces, when it is sensitive to their needs and aspirations, and when it effectively uses its resources to work with those partners to develop the full potential of this country. Sadly, sir, this textbook case of bungled federalism will be justified only if the government has learned that lesson.

Hear, hear!
Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce): In listening to the hon. member who has just taken her seat, Mr. Speaker, I could not help but think that it was delivered very well indeed, with just the right amount of indignation towards the government. It was a beautiful delivery. It is too bad the content was not as worthy as the effort the hon. member put into the delivery and the amount of indignation she expressed in her voice from time to time.
Let me just say a few things about Bill C-56 and perhaps give it its proper interpretation. First of all, the federal government, in bringing about the tax measures that it brought in on

April 10, went to great pains to seek out the co-operation of the ten provinces in Canada. For the first time in my history in parliament, a finance minister, before bringing down a budget, seriously talked at length to the finance ministers of the ten provinces. It was a tremendously innovative, daring and risky initiative. The hon. member talked about wanting a strong, effective, and dynamic government. Well, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) showed effectiveness, dynamism, and initiative in talking to the provincial finance ministers.
The purpose of the sales tax reduction was to stimulate the economy and to encourage Canadians to go out and shop now.
I would say buy now in Canada. Why did the Minister of Finance want to encourage that when profits were up in Canada in the last quarter of 1977 by 22 per cent and savings were up nearly an equal amount? It was because our factories and their efficiency were only at a production level of approximately 80 per cent. The idea was to encourage Canadians to buy, but not necessarily equally in all provinces. That was not the case. The Minister of Finance dealt with each province. He went out and consulted with each finance minister individually. One can look at the budget papers where it clearly states that he offered to compensate them for a reduction of 2 percentage points in their retail sales tax for a period of six months. He states:
In return, I have asked them to bear the cost of either a further one percentage point for the same period, or an extension of the two-point cut for a further three month period.
He clearly outlined what he wanted the provinces to accept. He went on to say that he recognized the Atlantic provinces were in a different position because of the tax and revenue structures of those provinces, and he also commented that he recognized that Alberta was in a different position.
Quebec, after consultations with Mr. Parizeau, its minister of finance, chose not to go along with the federal Minister of Finance. It was not the choice of the federal Minister of Finance, but a choice which was made by the province of Quebec. Is that such a strange thing for us federalists to believe? Was it completely unexpected that Quebec would not go along with the federal government? To me it was not unexpected because the government of Quebec today has stated quite clearly that they want to separate from Canada and that they want to do everything they can to prove to Canadians that federalism is not working. The choice was not that of the federal Minister of Finance but of the Quebec government, and if they had done anything else than what they did, I would have been surprised.
The federal Minister of Finance, however, did not remove any of the benefits in his budget for the people of Quebec. He did not in any way, but Mr. Parizeau did.
And Mr. Ryan too.

Mr. Parizeau was the one who prohibited the poor people from taking advantage of the offer made by the

Minister of Finance of the federal government, but he went on to give $40 million under the four items on which Mr. Parizeau said he would reduce the sales tax. It is perfectly within our constitution and within the prerogative of the minister of finance of a province to remove the sales tax completely if he so wishes. That is what Mr. Parizeau did, and there is nothing wrong with that.
This government asked for an across the board removal of the sales tax. Mr. Parizeau did not what to comply with this, and the Minister of Finance chose the most appropriate way to pay back to the people of Quebec the approximately $215 million which they would have had if the minister of finance of Quebec had accepted the offer.
There has been a lot of statements made about this country of ours and federalism. There is no question in my mind, in the 20 years that I have been in this House, that Canada, the very fact that we remain a nation, has been questioned very severely. It might well be that in this budget of April 10 we are once again seeing our country being questioned as a nation. The Minister of Finance has done his utmost.
I for one regret to see the official opposition wholeheartedly supporting Mr. Parizeau, the one who is deliberately attempting to divide and destroy this country. I am not surprised, however, because just a little over a year ago when I was in that party they told me to go easy on Mr. Levesque and not to attack him. They wanted him as an ally the next time a federal election rolled around. Maybe that explains why they are stoutly defending Mr. Parizeau today. Why I do not know; one can reach his own conclusions.
I know that the federal government has a responsibility for the over-all defence of the nation. I know, as a nation, that the federal government has a responsibility and that responsibility can be shared with the provinces with regard to the question of immigration.
I know, as a nation, we have a responsibility to provide a transportation system across Canada and at the ports. I know, as a nation, we have a responsibility to look after our trade, with other countries. I certainly know that, as a nation, we must have a strong, effective, dynamic minister of finance, and I think that is what we have in the present Minister of Finance. The finance of the nation is the very key and the heart of keeping a country together.
I know, and the budget dealt with it at length, that the question of energy has become of national importance to this country. It is of importance to every country in the world. As far as we can see in the foreseeable future, energy will remain of national importance to every nation, particularly Canada. We are in a very fortunate position, and I intend to deal with that point at length further on in my speech.
First of all I want to say a word about the differences that the Minister of Finance recognized in the field of taxation. In taking a look at personal income tax as it affects this country of ours, one can readily see that personal income tax as taxed by the provinces is a percentage of the basic federal tax. In the

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
province of Newfoundland it is 58 per cent of the basic federal tax. In the province of Quebec it varies slightly. Quebec levies its own income tax. Depending on how many children a married couple has, it varies from 58 per cent to 63 per cent of the basic federal tax. One could go down the list, but I want to cite Alberta's position and put it on the record. I will name only three provinces although I have the figures here for all of them. For the province of Alberta it is 38 per cent of the basic federal tax.
There is a logical reason why the Minister of Finance in his attempt to bring and hold our country together should address himself to the problem that exists in Canada, a huge tax rate in some provinces and a lower tax rate in other provinces. Similarly, in some provinces there is a high sales tax rate, and in another province there is no sales tax rate at all. The Minister of Finance, in my opinion, was quite right in addressing himself to that problem.
I want to deal now with another question. I read very carefully the speech of the finance critic for the opposition party. It was rather a poor speech, but he said this:
If it becomes the law of the land will not the residents of Alberta be taking the right position in saying they should be included?
That is why I wanted to put those tax figures on the record. What citizen of Alberta would not recognize that they have, by far, the lowest tax rate in Canada? If the Minister of Finance attempts to increase purchasing by increasing the purchasing power of citizens, to get our economy turned up a little more by lowering the sales tax by 2 per cent for a period of six months-
Don't be an Olson now, Jack.
Oh, oh!

the present Minister of Finance was neglecting Alberta and western Canada. How did he neglect western Canada when he was attempting to form the Bank of Western Canada?

We again have Sir Arthur riding to the rescue. He looks beautiful on the white horse with the hon. member for York-Simcoe. The beauty of those two hon. members is that they can ride a horse, which is more than the Leader of the Opposition can do.
In his whole speech the hon. member attempted to build on the premise that the Minister of Finance knew not what he was doing and was incapable of being Minister of Finance. This has been his whole line of attack. I was, as Your Honour correctly stated, nearly at the end of my remarks about the Bank of Western Canada.
The hon. member tried to run $195,000 into a pyramid and control $13 million-not a bad stroke of business if you can do it overnight. However, he was not able to do it.
He had called it the Bank of Western Canada. He wanted the deposits of western Canada. The interest rates were coming off. Where was the control going to be? It was to be held by a consortium of basically his family and two other people in the city of Toronto. He would not put 53 per cent on the market for sale. It was not because the remainder was not gobbled up. The nearly six and a half was gobbled up quickly. He kept control in Toronto and tried to perpetrate the belief that he was some kind of a saviour to western Canada and that he cared about western Canada. He cared about his own pocket and not much else at that time.
I want to say how Alberta has benefited in recent years and will continue to benefit by the budget of April 10.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I did not interrupt the minister when he was making certain comments concerning the formation of the Bank of Western Canada, but I hasten to add, in case anybody has inferred otherwise, there is not one tittle of truth in what he has said.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is not a question of privilege. What I said is on the Finance Committee records. What I said was supported by the former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. James Coyne, when he blew the whistle on the hon. member and said, "produce your $4V4 million," and he could not. I am not saying any untruths. It all can be substantiated and, in fact, has been substantiated in the past.
I wanted to deal with how the energy development incentives announced on April 10 will benefit the province of Alberta. Most Canadians are aware of the energy picture in the world today. I will paint the picture as vividly as I can so that Canadians can clearly understand.
In the known conventional oil reserves there are about 6.4 billion barrels of oil in Canada. We in this country use about
Income Tax Act
600 million barrels a year, or 1.6 million barrels a day. If someone looks at this speech tomorrow, he can use a computer or check my mathematics and he will see that we have in conventional oil reserves, if our consumption does not increase, somewhere between ten and 12 years' of known supplies.
What about the tar sands and the heavy oil, the development of which this budget attempted to encourage? In the tar sands in Alberta there is estimated to be 900 billion barrels of oil, a fabulous amount when you equate that to our conventional reserves. Three hundred billion barrels of oil can readily be mined in the tar sands if we put the capital investment into that area. With regard to the other 600 billion, we may have to develop new technology. We may have to develop a better in situ method of recovery. Of the 300 billion barrels I spoke of in the tar sands, about 80 per cent is recoverable with today's technology. Of the remaining 600 billion, with today's technology we can probably recover something in the neighbourhood of 15 to 20 per cent.
Looking at those Figures one can see how fortunate this country is, if we develop the tar sands quickly enough and have it coming on stream when our conventional oil begins to slow up.
We have a lead time of 12 years, at best 15. Therefore it behooves the federal government to encourage tar sands development now. Did the Minister of Finance take that into consideration in his budget? Yes he did, in about three different ways, and I will deal with them.
Outside of the conventional oil wells and the tar sands, we have in northeastern Alberta what is commonly referred to as the heavy oils. They are in the ground. The present method of bringing them up is to pump steam down which forces up the oil. In the known estimate of reserves of heavy oils, there is about 30 billion barrels of oil. Roughly speaking, we have five times the amount of reserves in the heavy oils and 150 times the amount in the tar sands that we have in the conventional wells.
There is only one other industrial country in the world today that can say down the road, if proper care is taken now, that it will be self-sufficient. We can become a major exporter of oil. We have that much. Action must be taken.
I am often accused of comparing our country with other countries. Today I want to compare our country with the United States with regard to the question of oil. One year ago the United States were using approximately 14.7 million barrels a day. Today they are using 17.1 million barrels a day. They have had a tremendously rapid increase in their consumption of oil. What has their production been? One year ago production in the United States was 8.7 million barrels a day. Today it is 8.1 million barrels a day. Their consumption has risen rapidly and their production has gone down nearly as rapidly.
This is a very fortunate country. Our consumption has not gone up as fast, and our production and our capabilities of producing have increased substantially. If Canadians ever

looked around, they would see we are at the bottom of the rainbow. This country is very, very fortunate.
What is the federal government doing through this budget which is being attacked, by innocent people, I believe, because they know not why they speak? Some of them know not why they are here, even from the province of Alberta. 1 have heard Albertans stand up in this House and say that Alberta is not helped in any way by this budget. How foolish can they be! How unknowing of the truth can they be of the province of Alberta?
Previous ministers of finance introduced in budgets, and the present Minister of Finance reinstated it again last fall, drilling exploration funds that individuals can put together to invest in oil and gas exploration in the province of Alberta. Individuals can get together and invest in gas exploration in Alberta. Why do I say in Alberta? It so happens that in our great nation between 83 per cent and 85 per cent of the oil industry is in Alberta.
This tax provision, allowing individuals to invest in drilling and exploration, brought tremendous funds into the province from all over Canada. The president of Ranger Oil told me when I was speaking with him recently that, as far as his company was concerned, it was the largest investment put together in Canada for a Canadian firm. I asked him, out of curiosity, where the money came from, and he said that, by and large, most of it came from people in Montreal. More than 100 investment funds had been put together to back exploration and drilling. Dome Petroleum, which has done such tremendously good work for Canada in the Arctic exploring for oil and gas in the Beaufort Sea, has put a fund together using the tax provision brought forward in the budget and extended by the present Minister of Finance.
In his present budget the Minister of Finance has recognized the importance of heavy oil and of the tar sands. The federal government has put together a research fund under which $2 million a year will be devoted to extending our knowledge, particularly of the tar sands, in the next five years.
The Syncrude project alone involved an expenditure of some $2 billion, and the contribution made by the federal government was 15 per cent, or $300 million. Mr. Speaker, that is more than Quebec is getting under this sales tax proposal. That province is getting something in the neighbourhood of $215 million. But Ottawa put $300 million into Syncrude, bringing the consortium together after Atlantic Richfield backed out. The project is now coming on stream and will produce something like 125,000 barrels a day. I estimate that Syncrude cost $2 billion. A large proportion of that money was spent within the province of Alberta. Wages and salaries of workers accounted for half the cost. That money was spent within the province, and those people pay income tax into the provincial treasury. And I am not taking into consideration, now, the royalties which the provincial government will receive on the sale of this oil, oil developed through the encouragement of the federal government.

Look at page 10 of this document under Energy Development Incentives. The Minister of Finance clearly spells out:
Second, it will be important to extract as much oil as technologically possible from all deposits. It has already been established that enhanced recovery systems can greatly increase total production. After today, therefore, special machinery, equipment and other facilities acquired for enhanced recovery systems-specifically, so-called "tertiary" recovery-will be able to earn depletion at a rate of $1 for every $2 of expenditure as compared to the normal earning rate of $1 for $3.
This change means substantially more revenue for Alberta because it will continue for a lot longer than six months. The sales tax reduction is only for six months. Let us keep things in perspective.
The budget went on to say:
Finally, earned depletion may be applied at present only to reduce taxable resource profits, and only up to a ceiling of 25 per cent. This provision will be significantly improved. Effective immediately, corporations may deduct depletion earned through certain qualifying investment in non-conventional oil projects up to the extent of 50 per cent of total income.
These two measures will greatly encourage investment in the tar sands and in heavy oils. Further, the minister states, as set out on page 10 of the budgetary papers:
I want to make clear that the up-grading plants to process the heavy oil produced from wells into a type of oil similar to conventional crude will be treated as a manufacturing facility, eligible for fast write-offs and the reduced tax rate.
All this gives us an idea of the immense amount of money which will be invested in Alberta as a result of the encouragement given in the budget. I suppose the oil industry is still not clear as to the interpretation of these tax measures or as to what their full effect will be, but there is no question in my mind that there will be far more potential benefit from the assistance given to the development of oil deposits in Alberta than from the total of the tax reduction, which amounts to around $1.1 billion.
In other words, these measures will mean more by way of financial benefit and encourage more investment in Alberta than all the other benefits seen in the budget for all the other provinces put together.
If this is correct, one might say, "Surely, this is too much to give one province?" Mr. Speaker, it is not going out to one province. It is benefiting the whole nation. We know that sooner or later we must develop these resources. Indeed, we could become energy sufficient, and if we develop the proper technology we could even become a major exporter of oil after 1995, I estimate.
What has all this meant to the province of Alberta? I am told that many people are envious of that wealthy province. Many say it was Premier Manning, through his connection with the Lord above us all, who put the oil below the surface of Alberta. Today, many newcomers believe it was Premier Lougheed who put the oil below the surface of the province. There are some in this House who believe that the prosperity of Alberta is the result of the way in which the affairs of the province have been managed by its present government.
Mr. Speaker, I am well connected with the present government of Alberta, and you might say I even have good relations with that government. But I am fair enough to realize that the

One can say that the Minister of Finance neglected Alberta in his April 10 budget, but if one wanted to be parochial and to divide Canada into regions, he could do that too. 1 do not particularly like that. I got into federal politics because I am a federalist. One could even accuse me of being a centralist.
