I have never claimed to be an expert on taxation problems and, indeed, I am not an expert on taxation problems, but I know there are certain basic principles which should be applied to test all taxation problems. These principles depend, in my judgment, on whether proposed tax changes tend toward more equality or more inequality, whether they benefit those who already have too much or whether they are calculated to assist those below the proverty line and those in urgent need. Judged by these tests I find the present bill totally

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
inadequate. I propose to deal with the sales tax later, but I wish first to speak about the bill as a whole.
In March of this year the National Council of Welfare, which hon. members know is a responsible and experienced group of Canadians, produced a report on taxation and the distribution of income. This report reveals a society, and I quote:
-which continues to be marked by vast inequalities of income-inequalities which condemn three millions of our citizens to lives of poverty in the midst of Canada's widespread affluence.
The income gap separating the richest and poorest 20 per cent of Canadians has grown enormously over the past 25 years, and this drastic increase has been at a time when Canada has been creating an elaborate multi-billion income security system. In 1976 the lowest income 20 per cent of Canadians received barely 4 per cent of the total national income. The highest 20 per cent-in other words, the same number of people at the top level-received more than 40 per cent, a share ten times as great as the poorest 20 per cent.
It is a striking fact that this picture has not changed relatively over the past quarter of a century. In 1951 the bottom fifth of Canadians received 4.4 per cent of the national income. Today those people receive 3.9 per cent. The top fifth got 42.8 per cent. Today those people receive 44 per cent.
The incomes of the lower 20 per cent in 1951 stood at $3,060 which, adjusted for inflation, was the equivalent in 1976 of $6,900. By 1976 the difference between the richest and poorest fifths had increased by $18,000. In other words, the gap had increased by over four and a half times in constant dollars. Despite all the rhetoric about the welfare state, our system of taxation and welfare has had no effect in tempering the overwhelming inequality of income distribution. The supposed levelling effect of the tax system has turned out to be a myth.
The income tax system is indeed progressive, but the tax system includes a great deal more than personal income tax. There are federal and provincial sales taxes, excise taxes, import duties, property taxes, provincial health insurance premiums, contributions to the Canada and Quebec pension plans, and unemployment insurance premiums. These are all taxes under another name. What, then, is the reason for this situation?
In 1972 the Economic Council of Canada found that over the lower portion of the income scale the system tends to contradict the ability to pay principle by taxing the poor at a higher rate than those who are better off. The effect of the few taxes that are progressive, such as the income tax, is completely offset by the remainder of taxes in the system. Most important, a host of new exemptions and reductions has been introduced into income tax, all provisions which give no benefit whatsoever to those too poor to pay taxes, only modest benefits to lower and middle income persons, and the greatest benefits to those with the highest income. In 1976 the National Council of Welfare issued a report discussing these exemptions and reductions. In that report, entitled "The Hidden Welfare System", they estimated the cost of just 17 of these tax

subsidies-there are more than 60 all told-at $6.4 billion, with the taxpayer making over $50,000 a year receiving an average of $4,000 in annual benefits, and the taxpayer with less than $10,000 income receiving less than $500.
Much has been said about equity in the tax system. The scrutiny to which it has been put by the National Council of Welfare suggests that no such equity exists. I say-this is something that all of us from all parties in the House should know-that we in this country, despite all the good things we say about ourselves, despite the good fortune which we enjoy, have created a society in which there are gross injustices and inequalities along the lines which I have not dug up but which are based upon the report of the National Welfare Council.
To remedy this would require amendments to the methods of securing funds for the Canada and Quebec pension plans, unemployment insurance, and health care plans. The report of the National Council of Welfare goes into these in detail, but I will not do so here. Let me only remark that we in this party have supported and do support the welfare provisions. Indeed, we take some responsibility for their introduction. However, I will say that we too have underestimated the importance of making sure that the acquisition of funds or payment of these schemes is supported progressively rather than regressively, and adds to rather than diminishes the income of the poorer people. Nor is the objective of more equality merely a moral or humanitarian objective. It is not an objective of people of soft hearts and kind dispositions. It is a condition of a healthy economy?
With hundreds of thousands of Canadians below the poverty line, these Canadians are effectively debarred from playing an effective part in our market system. The net result of this unfair contribution of income is the state of depression, recession, and stagnation with which we are all familiar. The government plans in the tax bill with which we are dealing have failed to make any effective dent in these facts.
I want to return for a minute or two to the sales tax and the means devised to distribute the compensation benefits from the sales tax reductions. It is well known that the sales tax is one of the important means of taxation of the provinces. The provinces have claimed, and no doubt have the right to claim, the right to dispose of the proceeds of direct sales tax according to their own judgment and without interference from the federal government. The present legislation contemplates an intrusion in this field by the federal government. In so far as the provinces agree to this and accept federal leadership, there can be no objection, but interference over the objection of the provinces is interference in a provincial field which is highly important to our whole federal system. In the case of Quebec and the other provinces, the federal government offered to repay compensation equivalent to the reduction in the sales tax and the losses from that across the whole field. This has been accepted with varying degrees of grumbling from all the provinces except the province of Quebec.
May 24, 1978

The Quebec government preferred a scheme where there should be a total abolition of the sales tax for certain essential commodities. I think it included textiles, furniture, etc. I will not go through the list, but they are unquestionably essentials. This reduction was to be a total reduction, not limited in time, and obviously presented a real contrast to the proposals made by the federal government. However, the purpose of these reductions was to promote employment, which is the objective of the exercise claimed by the federal government. It provided for the stimulation of employment through reduction in the prices of the goods covered by the tax. The federal government has obstinately refused to pay compensation, as requested by the government of Quebec, except in the form of direct payments to the citizens of Quebec who pay income tax.
The federal proposal has earned the opposition of the government of Quebec and all the other parties in the legislative assembly of Quebec, of all the opposition parties in the House of Commons, and some opposition from other provinces. The federal government has persisted in its particular plan with an obstinacy worthy of a better cause.
There may be arguments as to whether the federal or Quebec scheme for the reduction of the sales tax is best. I myself prefer the Parizeau to the Chretien model, and one of the basic reasons for that is that the federal scheme excludes the most needy of all, the people who do not earn enough even to have to pay any income tax, those who are on the poverty line and who do not benefit, even though they still have to pay sales tax on what they purchase. It is here that the general principle which I outlined at the beginning of my speech is applicable, namely, that all tax proposals should be judged by the effect on the poorest people in the community. But the real tragedy is that this comes at a time when the federal government claims to give leadership to strengthening and preserving our federal system.
What the federal government has proposed gives aid and comfort to separatists, and is a blow to the future of Canada. Furthermore, it appears to violate the government's own proposed guidelines on conditional grants for federal-provincial programs. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has dealt with this matter and I will not repeat what she said but will summarize some of the points in my own way.
In 1969 the Government of Canada issued, under the signature of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself, a constitutional working paper entitled "Federal-Provincial Grants and the Spending Power of Parliament". The white paper stated that the proposed principles would establish two limitations on the use by parliament of its power to make conditional grants for general federal-provincial programs. Of course these schemes for the sales tax are precisely that because the Government of Canada, quite rightly, is going to spend the money and was asking that the moneys received be applied to the sales tax.
According to the white paper on the federal proposal, first, there must be the existence of a broad national consensus in favour of the program, and second, there must be the assur-
Income Tax Act
ance that a fiscal penalty would not be imposed on the people of non-participating provinces. I note the constitutional paper refers to people and not governments. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and others would claim that looking after the claims of the people of Quebec and bypassing the provincial government is in accordance with the guidelines proposed. I do not think the guidelines intended any such thing. The people of Quebec, as selected by the federal government, may well not be the same people as those who would benefit from a disposition of the funds by the provincial legislature.
Undoubtedly it is the constitutional right of the Quebec legislature to prefer to receive the payments in lieu of sales tax. In my understanding of our constitutional system, the federal government communicates in such matters with provincial governments and not with individuals in the provinces. All the preliminary papers I have read constantly refer to the provinces. Our system is composed of a federal parliament and provincial legislatures which are supreme within their own realms. This is not a new doctrine. It was pronounced by learned law lords in the privy council of Great Britain, which was the final court of appeal, nearly a century ago. The provincial legislatures have sovereign rights within their own jurisdictions.
The constitutional paper produced by the Prime Minister goes on to suggest that the first step toward ensuring a consensus would be the introduction in parliament of a money resolution preceding a bill to be proceeded with if and when a consensus was reached. This has not been done yet. Obviously it may be done in the future. It was contemplated to be the first step. Then this resolution was to be sent to each province for approval or rejection in their legislatures. That was contained in the statement of the Prime Minister on behalf of the government when the future constitution of Canada was being dealt with.
The Minister of Finance has not come close to following the proposed method of operation of the federal government. One must assume the federal government is abandoning its own scheme of instituting a federal plan for conditional grants to the provinces. As this is a central feature of federal-provincial relations, greater attention should have been paid to it by the government. Its failure to do so constitutes a blow to the unity of Canada and a blow to Canada itself.
Now I should like to turn to the other provisions of Bill C-56. As I read them, apart from the corporate sales tax, there is little or nothing designed to assist those in the greatest need, or to equalize the distribution of income. Clause 1 of the bill deals with the removal of taxes and expenses of a second residence needed for temporary purposes. Perhaps this is a good idea, but it is hardly an important one. Clause 4 deals with loans to shareholders by corporations. Certainly it is not an earth-shaking measure. Clause 6 deals with additional allowances for scientific research. Indeed this is needed and beneficial, but it can hardly be said to have any direct impact

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
upon the distribution of income. Clause 11 and other clauses deal with registered retirement income funds. The proposals in clause 11 may be a measure of relief for those who contribute to these funds. Perhaps much of the clause can be commended. Elowever, it encourages saving and not spending. To that extent it fails to stimulate employment, which is a major priority of the day.
Clause 14 deals with the transfer by a taxpayer to his child resident in Canada of shares of a qualifying farm corporation. Indeed this is a helpful provision, but it is of very little significance in the over-all picture. Clause 30 deals with the reduction in 1978 of the tax payable by individual residents in prescribed provinces by $100. Indeed this may have some small effect on stimulating purchasing power, but it would be far more effective in redistributing income equitably if income taxes were used and if it were removed entirely from those at the lowest level.
I cannot say that I have read the bill carefully, but I have glanced at the 66 pages which constitute the involved provisions before us. Also I have read the notice of the ways and means motion to summarize some of the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act. The same observation is true of nearly all of these provisions. Some of them may remedy minor injustices, but none of them provide an adequate stimulation of the economy by making more purchasing power available, none of them reduce the enormous gap between rich and poor in the country.
My party has made its stand very clear. It believes it is necessary to fulfil these dual purposes: on the one hand, the stimulation of the economy and reduction of unemployment and, on the other hand, more justice in our tax system and a redistribution of income by income tax reductions at lower levels. The government has not taken this advice although many others, as well as the New Democratic Party, advocated this course.
For these reasons I cannot support this bill. It might be said cynically but justly, as my party is against the bill, as I work with the party and attempt to support it when I can, that my vote against the bill is no more than a party vote. Indeed it is a party vote, but it is much more than that. It is an endeavour to express my regret that the government has failed to stimulate the economy adequately, to deal effectively with unemployment so far as the tax system can and, above all, has failed to maintain the principle of a more just and fair distribution of income in Canada to those who are at the poverty line or below.
Also, the government has failed to reduce the gap between those who have acquired substantial and secure incomes in Canada and those who live in poverty. In my view, this is the essence of this legislation. It is ample reason for saying it is not good enough, if we are truly concerned about the welfare of all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to bring my humble contribution to the second reading of Bill C-56, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions. I do not claim to be an expert in taxation or even in constitutional law, but I think I know the problems of Quebec as much as the member who had the floor before me, and I will try to be practical regarding the study of the bill.
To start with, Mr. Speaker, I will confess that I have never felt so surprised in seeing the attitude of the members of the opposition because the issue is to sell a sales tax reduction to all Canadians. There is nothing about increasing taxes, and yet it seems that we are experiencing difficulties in getting people to accept a lower sales tax. I hope that my intervention will not be considered and interpreted by some as an interference into provincial jurisdiction or as the attitude of a traitor to the people of Quebec or even as that of an unconditional federalist. Rather I am appealing to my fellow citizens from Quebec so that they will consider my intervention as that of a representative of Quebec who had been elected to the House of Commons and has the courage of defending his convictions, who believes in the Liberal philososphy and wishes to continue improving the standard and quality of living of his fellow citizens in the city of Laval, in the province of Quebec and all accross this country by supporting a program designed to meet a most difficult economic situation not only in Quebec or even in Canada but in all industrial countries of the world. Throughout my speech, I will endeavour to point out the reasons which justify Bill C-56 while trying to provide some explanations on the crippling attitude of finance minister Parizeau, and also voice my opposition to a general transfer from government to government for if we consider the objectives of this legislation a general transfer cannot reach them.
This bill is in line with the main measures deriving from the economic and fiscal statement made before the Commons on October 20 of last year. Under this initiative from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), Canadians have benefited from a $100 income tax reduction for the months of January and February. Altogether this amounted to a reduction of some $700 million which, coupled with the indexation factor of 7.2 per cent, represented another saving, or if you prefer another federal government revenue loss, a saving of $850 million for Canadians. The April 10 Chretien budget reflects this trend by offering the provinces a reduction in their sales tax. The two-thirds compensation by the Canadian government comes in addition to the $700 million which I mentioned earlier, so to these $850 million granted through indexation we are adding another contribution of some $1,147 billion, namely the value of the proposed reduction of the retail sales tax.

May 24, 1978

The budget is a positive reform in the context of our current economic problems, increasing as it does the consumer's purchasing power and the level of production of a number of our manufacturers who are now using some 60 per cent of their capacity. So we are increasing our industrial production, which will in turn foster job creation. Mr. Speaker, the sales tax reduction initiative has been supported and indeed called for by a number of economic groups. As an illustration, I would like to quote from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce report, Impact, Vol. 2, No. 3, the March 1978 bulletin issued when the Canadian Chamber of Commerce came here to Ottawa to meet with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay):
If the Canadian government feels it has an absolute duty to stimulate the economy, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce believes the best way would be a 2 to 3 per cent reduction of provincial sales taxes. In the pre-budget brief issued in Ottawa on March 6, the chamber indicates it can easily be proven the government should maintain the size of its deficit...
And it goes on with a number of other suggestions. I would once more quote a paragraph from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce submission to minister Chretien:
But in order to absorb the high unemployment rate and the serious underutilization forecast for the Canadian economy this year, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce recommends that the federal and provincial governments share equally in the provincial sales tax reduction. However, Ottawa should pay an extra percentage point in areas where unemployment is above the national average. The chamber feels that such reductions will meet a number of prerequisites for a real economic pickup.
That proposition was put forward by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I heard no member indicate this was suggested by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, an important group in our Canadian economy. I would also have welcomed associations and chambers of commerce from various Quebec towns and cities if they also had been in support of the Minister of Finance's initiative at the suggestion of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I also have here, Mr. Speaker, another report on the conference of industry, trade and commerce ministers, a federal-provincial conference held here in Ottawa. That document was signed by Mr. Rodrigue Tremblay, the Quebec minister of industry and commerce. I am quoting from page 5 of the magazine Commerce of April 1978:
Precise and immediate actions needed.
Care should be taken however that, under the pretext of discussing medium and long-term industrial strategies, concrete and immediate steps needed to correct the most urgent problems are not neglected. The Canadian manufacturing sector is probably more seriously affected by the current economic recession than other sectors of the economy.
Due to insufficient demand, most companies are now experiencing below normal capacity utilization. Demand stimulation measures therefore appear to be urgently needed to strengthen the manufacturing sector.
We would be doing a real disservice to companies and workers if, in the course of such a conference-
Income Tax Act
This was the January conference-
-we simply discuss medium and long-term strategies. It is imperative that each level of government take concrete and immediate steps to stabilize and strengthen employment in the manufacturing sector.
So, Mr. Speaker, there you have Quebec's position as stated by its minister of industry and commerce, Mr. Rodrigue Tremblay, after a federal-provincial conference of ministers of industry, trade and commerce.
So the budget is indeed a positive response to representations. It is an answer to the representations made either by the chamber of commerce or by other organizations in the economic sector-and even trade and commerce minister Tremblay agreed-to do something to stimulate consumer activity. The Chretien budget is a positive reform for economic problems. It has many elements. I referred earlier to the sales tax and I shall come back to this later on, but the budget is also an incentive for industrial development. As the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) said this afternoon, it is an incentive for research and development, and will have short term and long term effects on investments, productivity and employment. These measures are essential to reinforce the position of Canada in an increasingly competitive world.
The third and not the least aspect of this budget which we sometimes forget to mention is the expansion in the field of social legislation of the possibilities offered to the two million individuals who contribute to a registered retirement savings plan and the creation for those who reach retirement age of a new plan for accumulated savings which will be called the registered retirement income fund. I am somewhat disappointed to see that my colleague who spoke before me did not even mention this benefit contained in the budget. The budget also contains other measures such as the extension to incorporated farms of the tax free transfer of farming operations, which now applies only to members of the same family. Mr. Speaker, those are the main features of the Chretien budget, which also includes the firm commitment to reduce federal expenditures by $350 million. How have the various sectors of the Canadian economy reacted to this budget?
Chretien budget favourably received by Canadian business sectors.
Despite a small group of dissatisfied business interests, most Canadian business sectors quickly applauded yesterday the federal budget introduced Monday evening by finance minister, Jean Chretien.
We fully endorse the fiscal co-operation between provincial and federal governments which has made sales tax cuts possible, stated the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
This measure will help create jobs because Canadians will buy more Canadian products and it will also result in lower prices at the consumer level.
Chamber of commerce chairman Sam Hughes, to whom I referred the representations made to the Minister of Finance last January, said about the last budget:
Mr. Chr6tien has taken the "basic measures that were required".
According to him,...

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
... the chairman of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce ...
... sales tax cuts will do much to eliminate regional disparities and will encourage demand at the consumer level "where it is required".
Mr. Hughes believes that Mr. Chretien was right not to reduce personal income tax as it would have interfered with capital inflow into government coffers.
The Chairman of the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen, Mr. John Bulloch, said that the last budget showed fiscal creativity and emphasized that the government did its best with little money. Those are a few comments on this budget from various organizations in the private sector.
The budget, as presented, has surely answered the wishes of several organizations to which I have referred and it is obvious that it cannot get the unanimous approval of all those individuals. The budget has even succeeded in suggesting steps likely to increase the total demand of the Canadian economy. Following meetings and consultations with the provinces, the budget is the first step towards the distribution of responsibilities between the two levels of government as regards the stabilization policy and more especially the economic stimulus.
Rather than being an intrusion into provincial autonomy, the budget provisions reflect the importance of divided responsibilities as a result of economic conditions. As stated on several occasions by the Minister of Finance, we must bear in mind that 60 per cent of taxes in Canada are levied by provinces and municipalities while 40 per cent are collected by the federal government. It is therefore impossible for the federal government to take full responsibility for the employment situation and to implement alone an economic stabilization policy without the provinces' co-operation.
This situation is most obvious, it seems to me, in the Chretien-Parizeau dispute, especially since in negotiations, with a separatist government whose "raison d'etre" is to leave Canada, and solutions are apt to be slow in coming. The aim of the Quebec government is precisely to show the people of that province that it is impossible to live under a federal system. Mr. Levesque said in October 1967, and I quote, as I think this is extremely important in the context of this debate:
A sovereign Quebec assumes all powers and all financial resources of the public sector. Thus it has all the tools of decision and the total product of its fiscal efforts.
Today, this same Mr. Levesque goes to the United States, Mr. Morin to London and others to African countries who are stating that this is a sovereignty association. It is therefore not surprising that negotiations between the province of Quebec and the Minister of Finance cannot take the form of a dialogue as with the other provinces. Mr. Speaker, it seems as difficult to come to an understanding with the P6quiste government on the sharing of goods and obliglations as it is to reconstitute the eggs from an omelet. That is an absolutely impossible task, Mr. Speaker. Quebec sells more manufactured goods to other provinces than it buys from them and most of its sales consist of highly protected products such as clothing and footwear. To

substantiate this, one has only to look at the latest figures published in this regard and which show that Quebec does indeed sell more manufactured products to the rest of Canada than it buys from the other provinces. In textiles, for instance, sales are in the range of S192 million.
In the furniture industry, $134 million. In clothing, $503 million. In the leather industry, $59 million. In textiles, $111 million. In this whole sector, products worth $1 billion are manufactured in Quebec and sold in the rest of Canada. Quebec also sells a high percentage of its products in the other provinces, for example 41 per cent in the rubber industry, the leather industry 47.8 per cent, textile industry 38.6 per cent, knitted wear industry 39.4 per cent, clothing industry 41.7 per cent and furniture industry 40.2 per cent.
What would be the consequences if the other provinces did not cut their taxes on these products? The crippling attitude of Quebec finance minister Parizeau might very well balkanize the provinces. There are other products which are made in Quebec and on which there is absolutely no sales tax cut. I have in mind the refrigerator and range industries in l'As-somption which are providing jobs to some 400 people. In the area of electric lamps, Westinghouse is providing jobs to 600 people in Trois-Rivieres. I have also in mind sporting goods and cooking ware industries in Cowansville, Cookshire, Drum-mondville, and trailer manufacturers in Cookshire, and many other firms which are being penalized because they cannot cut the sales tax by the amount suggested in Mr. Parizeau's budget. I am also thinking of electric controls in Granby and cars in Sainte-Therese, with some 3,000 people employed, near my riding. It seems to me that these figures should matter to us, that Quebec also benefits from some products, and that several of the sectors which were meant to be protected were already protected by a number of measures to which I will now refer.
In light of those statistics and the request of representatives of various economic sectors, the Chretien budget was definitely a necessity. But the situation deteriorated after Quebec finance minister Parizeau refused the Chretien proposal for reducing the sales tax across the board and suggested instead that the cut apply only to furniture, clothing and textiles. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I was very disappointed with minister Parizeau who, instead of congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for having consulted the provinces before preparing his budget, accused him of interfering with provincial budgets.
Mr. Speaker, that is an opinion to which I have given a lot of thought. I am a Quebecker, I was born in Quebec, and I find that language problems are not the only source of confrontation between Canadians: there are also problems of power. Cultural, social and economic problems become political as soon as one wonders which government has authority to solve them. That may be even truer in Quebec. The problem of the sharing of powers is fundamental to any given society. The
May 24, 1978

political aspect is important but basically sharing of power is much more important, more dramatic than sharing of powers.
Mr. Parizeau's refusal to co-operate in economic matters was given support by several provincial groups of constitutional experts that are less competent in the economic and financial field than the organizations which 1 referred to at the outset of my speech. And yet, being an economist, Mr. Pari-zeau must know that the economy of any country cannot be dissociated and that it is a joint responsibility of the federal government and the provinces to stimulate the economy by appropriate measures.
It is obvious that the sales tax comes under provincial jurisdiction. Some people are still pointing that out as if the Minister of Finance was not even aware of it. That is precisely why he spent three weeks negotiating with the provinces and that eight out of ten agreed because he knew perfectly well it was a provincial jurisdiction. The sales tax does belong to the provinces but they are not losing anything because the federal government is prepared to pay two thirds of the total cost of the proposed reduction. General reduction of the sales tax on all products in all provinces should increase demand for consumer goods. We should recall that in his budget of April 1975 Ontario finance minister McKeough allowed a 2 per cent sales tax reduction until December of the same year.
Retail sales in Ontario had increased by 14 per cent in that year, i.e. 2 per cent over and above the Canadian average. All the stores have shown a certain amount of prosperity with increased sales of goods. The Chretien proposal has seemed so interesting for the Quebec government which had identified itself a few months ago with levying tax on children's clothing and shoes that today, being conscious of their error, they have taken through their minister Parizeau this opportunity to exempt clothing, shoes and even furniture. And the federal tax on children's clothing had been completely removed at the wholesaler's level three years ago. The imagination of finance minister Parizeau had been involved to a greater extent in the levying of taxes on children's clothing and shoes than with any reduction of sales tax. Has minister Chretien's proposal led minister Parizeau to think about removing that sales tax that he had himself initiated for Quebeckers?
Given its economic objective, the Canadian government has committed itself along with the provinces to overcoming unemployment, creating jobs and straightening out the economy all across Canada. They therefore suggested to the Canadian provinces a reduction in consumer sales tax for all manufactured goods sold by any busines or store, for any retail sale. Recently, I met a group of manufacturers, at an exhibition held in Quebec. Naturally, I was asked what was my reaction, my attitude to the Parizeau proposal as against the Chretien budget? They were manufacturers at an exhibition. I told them: "I will reply by asking you a question. You will then say that it is the way a politician answers but I would rather be a political man of action than be called a politician." I asked
Income Tax Act
how many of the 126 participants in this exhibition were displaying footwear and clothes? Not a single one. This means that none of those manufacturers could benefit from the sales tax reduction, because Mr. Parizeau has decided to act on a selective basis rather than reduce the sales tax on all manufactured goods. I think that this somehow describes the situation of our industries in Quebec. They are being penalized by the action of Mr. Parizeau.
Alberta-a province that has no retail sales tax, and one of the three Canadian provinces contributing to equalization payments, which Quebec will receive this year to the tune of $1,350 billion, that is, 45 per cent of the total amount- accepted the Chretien proposal, and not necessarily to benefit from it, because there is no sales tax in Alberta, without receiving the contribution of the Canadian government. That participation, it seems to me, which amounts to $186 million in Quebec, is precisely the federal contribution for the 2 per cent cut in the retail sales tax.
It is unfortunate that millions of Quebec consumers, thousands of Quebec manufacturers, and hundreds of Quebec businessmen and dealers should be penalized because of the attitude of minister Parizeau who restricts the tax cut to textiles, clothing and shoes. I checked whether sheets made in the Eastern Townships, sheets and pillow cases made in Quebec would be tax free, and found they would not. The reason why the sales tax applies is that the goods covered by the Parizeau budget include only yard goods and not sheets, pillow cases and things like that. Yet, all goods imported from Taiwan and manufactured abroad will not be taxed. So, I feel it is unfortunate that millions of consumers, manufacturers and dealers in Quebec should be penalized because of that decision.
The implementation of selective tax cuts will not be an easy matter. It is not easy to monitor retail stores nowadays, shops which sell combs, dishes, tires, paint, electric appliances, and even sweaters imported from Taiwan. The Chretien formula cut the sales tax on all the products sold. The Chretien formula applied to all products; it is much simpler and much more direct for all consumers, including those who have no taxable income, which means those who do not pay income tax.
If we changed the formula, it is because of Mr. Parizeau's refusal. It is rather the formula of the Quebec finance minister, a tax measure, which balkanizes the Quebec industry. This late proposal by Mr. Parizeau, being discriminatory, could result in a balkanization of the Canadian economy, it could paralyze the retail sales industry and penalize the consumers in Quebec. I think a responsible government which wants to negotiate an association with the other provinces of Canada should act in a less selfish, not to say in a less separatist manner.
I hope that during this debate we shall make the people in Quebec realize what this dispute means and how important it

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
is that the Government of Canada develop with the provinces a sound climate of co-operation, if we want to solve together the economic problems in the country and continue to improve the situation of the population which should not be penalized by this dispute. Let us stop bringing politics into the economy, because in so doing, we distort the mechanisms at the expense of all taxpayers, both in the business world, in industry and for the consumers.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-56 I would like to put on record some of my reservations about the way the minister has handled the provincial tax situation. First, although our expenditures are some $45 billion, with an $11.5 billion deficit, the minister and the government have shown their ineptitude by getting involved in a measure that has only created confusion and consternation. It is doing nobody any good, while the country suffers. I do not disagree but that it is a reasonable tax change as regards sales tax if it could be administered easily, but in our complex federal system it is obvious from the beginning that it was a maze of contradictions, difficult to administer and still more difficult to institute.
The previous member spoke of economists and businesses and suggested that this sales tax abatement is a good idea. I agree, but not in our complex federal system. Furthermore, many of the negotiations seem to have been by telephone and, unless they are recorded, there is no record but merely the verbal recall of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) of the various provinces.
This is interesting because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance suggested they had long consultations with the four western premiers and with Mr. Parizeau. However, these gentlemen generally denied there were any great consultations. In the case of Manitoba, they were more or less told, rather than there being negotiations.
Given the situation in Quebec, Mr. Parizeau has roundly outfoxed the Minister of Finance, and the federal government will be putting up some $ 140 million more money from general revenues, according to my calculation, than what it would have if the government had followed the same course with Quebec as it has followed with Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia, the so-called provinces that have economic stability. The dilemma of the government can be best summarized by the editorial in the Globe and Mail of May 18, and I quote:
The federal government has done what nobody thought could be done. It has united the Quebec National Assembly. It has induced all members of all parties in that assembly to denounce as "totally unacceptable" the federal response to the Quebec government's refusal to cut its sales tax to fit federal demands. It has produced a unanimous request from the assembly to members of all parties in parliament, including members of the Liberal party, to oppose the federal legislation which would grant tax rebates to Quebec taxpayers in place of the across-the-board cut in provincial sales tax which the Quebec government has refused to make.
Even Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau virtually admitted that his government was in the wrong. "The federal government" he told the House, "should not use

tax leverage over the provinces to force a province to do certain things." He tried to contend that Mr. Chretien had not done such a thing because he had consulted the provinces for three weeks before he brought in his budget which guaranteed that Ottawa would pick up two-thirds of the cost of a temporary across-the-board reduction in sales taxes if the provinces would pick up the other one-third.
Yet on budget night Mr. Chretien himself admitted that Quebec had not agreed to the deal. And Quebec did not agree to the deal. It decided instead to eliminate the sales tax entirely on certain items that are chiefly produced in Quebec, thus providing maximum stimulation to the Quebec economy. That was within its right.
In the Montreal Gazette of May 18 we have what I think is a very good account of the problems of the Minister of Finance in dealing with Mr. Parizeau. It had always been my impression that the Minister of Finance had the tacit approval of Mr. Parizeau when he introduced the controversial sales tax measure. But instead, he, Mr. Parizeau, did something entirely different than what the rest of the nine provinces have done.
In effect, the provinces of the rest of Canada, where they have sales taxes, reduced their sales tax by 3 per cent. This, in effect, helped the manufacturing industry mainly in Canada rather than any specific region, and I think it allowed the province of Quebec, more than any other, relative advantage.
According to Mr. Cam Nappi of the University of Montreal, as recorded in the Gazette of May 17, Quebec manufacturers would lose 30 per cent of their existing market while manufacturers in the rest of the country would lose only 10 per cent of their existing market. This heavy dependence of Quebec manufacturers on the rest of the country is because of two things. The rest of the country represents a larger market than Quebec alone, but it also means Quebec is more heavily depending on markets in other parts of the country than any of the other four regions in Canada. He went on to state that although statistics of interprovincial trade are incomplete, Quebec is, and I quote:
-the only region for which the Canadian market is more important than the international market.
Fifty six per cent of Quebec exports go elsewhere in Canada while 44 per cent go to other countries. He estimates that Quebec manufacturing exports over 100,000 Quebec jobs to Ontario while Ontario exports to Quebec about the same number of jobs. Canadian tariff barriers have strongly benefited Quebec manufacturers because industry in that province is concentrated in sectors protected by the highest tariff walls. Exports from Quebec to other provinces are protected by tariffs averaging 9.9 per cent, exports from Ontario averaging 8.4 per cent, and those from other provinces averaging 7.8 per cent.
By the Quebec action of the selective tariff cuts, they have in fact benefited most industries concentrated in those provinces, but the exports of Quebec manufactured goods will benefit from the reduced sales tax in all other parts of the country that have taken up the federal offer.
There has been complaining by the provincial premiers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia that there was not enough consultation, and that now a new ballgame has developed that is inimical to their interests. I certainly agree, but I wonder why the provincial governments were hood-
May 24, 1978

winked into agreeing with the Minister of Finance when he invaded their provincial jurisdictions on this short term episode.
Provincial jurisdictions have been invaded in the past through unemployment insurance, old age pensions, health and welfare programs forced on the provinces by the federal government and too expensive for efficient running of these programs. I might add that I believe one of the problems of disunity in this country is the fact that in the last 25 years the federal government has invaded provincial jurisdiction through massive health and welfare programs. This has caused much disunity in this country.
It is folly for the Minister of Finance to invade once again provincial jurisdiction without having very clear outlines as to what was at stake. He has done confederation a great disservice. His complaint in the budget speech that the federal government was losing control of the fiscal responsibility is not quite true. He points out that in 1945 the provincial sector had only 30 per cent of total government revenues whereas it now is 60 per cent. He further states that the provincial and municipal sector actually holds a larger share of total government revenues than does the federal government. But this argument is falacious because most of the increase in terms of percentages has been in the fields of health, welfare and education; in the last 20 years provincial governments have taken over from private plans, and the financing of these very expensive programs has fallen on the provincial governments instead of upon individuals. Some 60 per cent or more of provincial revenues are spent in the health field so the argument put forward by the minister is not valid.
I turn, now to the complex question of cash rebates to the citizens of Quebec. I can understand the contention of the Prime Minister that in the absence of a tax arrangement with Quebec the rebate must be different. But the decision to give a cash rebate to citizens of Quebec in the next few weeks smacks of political opportunism. In Manitoba, when income tax forms are made out in 1979 for 1978 tax, there will be a box in which citizens of that province will be able to claim a rebate of $100 on their 1978 tax from the federal government and, correspondingly, this amount will be taken up by the $100 recovery tax on the provincial side. Why does the federal goverment not reduce the $100 or its equivalent, $85 or whatever it is, on the tax returns for 1978 to be filed in Quebec next year? This would bring them in line with the other provinces.
The Minister of Finance accused Mr. Parizeau of bad taste. But in the matter of payment to Quebeckers it seems to me the Minister of Finance is just as guilty. Cash payments to Quebeckers will induce them to feel they should vote for the Liberal administration in October, if there is an election, and presumably, also, with the referendum coming up in Quebec, citizens of that province will look to Ottawa as a benevolent institution giving them payments they would not otherwise receive.
Income Tax Act
This must explain Mr. Parizeau's objection, because obviously the total economy of Quebec gains relatively more than the rest of the country. Mr. Parizeau has made selective tax cuts which will presumably effectively minimize the benefits to goods produced in the rest of the country and also to imports which in our financial position is its only saving grace. But Quebec industry will be able to benefit from the tax cuts in all the other parts of the country and their industries should get a relatively greater improvement than industry in other parts of the country.
Now what about the selective tax cuts? In these the federal government has assumed, I believe, that at 3 per cent applied across the board in Quebec as in other provinces they would have cost the Quebec treasury some $330 million, assuming the estimates given are correct, and I would assume that they are probably rough in nature. However, the selective tax cuts will presumably diminish the Quebec treasury by only some $120 million during the six months that the federal plan remains in force, so that the federal government says that it must make up $220 million to be even with the other provinces. Having allowed a $40 million credit for the selective tax cuts, the federal government proposes to pay $186 million to the citizens of Quebec. Assuming that all citizens of Canada paid approximately the same federal tax, the citizens of Quebec would have paid in some 25 per cent of $186 million, or some $45 million.
In the other provinces such as Ontario and Manitoba the provincial treasurers gave up 3 per cent of their sales tax income with 2 per cent reimbursed by their own citizens through the abatement of the federal tax system, and in the province of Quebec the provincial treasurer should have given up $330 million, as I understand the minister's calculations but, in fact, they are only giving up some $120 million, at least for the lifetime of the six months' agreement.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the rest of Canada is putting up some $140 million through the cash rebates to Quebec citizens over and above what the Quebec people themselves paid to the federal tax. It should be understood that during the lifetime of the agreement of six months, which is the only thing we are talking about, the provincial treasury of Quebec will not lose nearly the revenue that they would have under the across the board 3 per cent reduction. This represents a transfer from one portion of the country to the Quebec economy and a form presumably of equalization. I do not necessarily disagree with this but I should recognize it is a form of equalization payment.
I do not disagree one whit with the right of Quebec to impose selective tax cuts, but it is probably wrong to extend some form of federal subsidy hidden under the guise of sales tax rebates. I think it would have been better to allow the tax reduction to the Quebec taxpayer at the time he Filed his

May 24, 1978
Income Tax Act
income tax return for 1978. Taxation would have fallen more evenly across the country.
One of our taxation problems in this country is that justice must be seen to be done, it must not only be done. When taxpayers in different parts of the country are taxed differently-
